To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sputum levels of reduced glutathione increase 24 hours after allergen challenge only in isolated early asthmatic responders.
sputum GSH increased 24 h post allergen challenge in EAR but not in LAR asthmatic subjects, and that the GSSG proportion was correlated with eosinophils.

(1) GSH increases 6 h after allergen in isolated early asthmatics; (2) GSSG increases 6 h in both isolated early and dual responders, and correlates with sputum eosinophil counts in all subjects; (3) there was no difference in baseline GSH or GSSG between isolated early and dual asthmatic responders; and (4) there was no change in sputum nitrosothiol levels after allergen challenge.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lack of evidence to support the use of glutathione as an antioxidant supplement in the prevention or treatment of asthma.
the antioxidant glutathioine increases in the airways 24 hours after allergen challenge, only in isolated early asthmatics.
the GSH levels increase after allergen challenge only in EAR subjects, but the GSH levels in LAR subjects are similar before and after challenge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown for the first time that GSH levels are increased after allergen challenge only in patients with an isolated early response.
the increase of GSH 24 hours after allergen challenge is a marker for an isolated EAR.
the increase in reduced glutathione 24 h after an allergen challenge is associated with isolated early asthmatic responses, whereas dual asthmatics do not show such a pattern.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GSH is increased after early asthmatic reactions, but not late asthmatic responses, and this may contribute to the different pathophysiologies underlying these reactions.
the levels of GSH are higher in isolated early asthmatic responders, but not dual responders.
